title: Short Stuff: Trovants
summary: Short Stuff episode on trovants (also spelled trovants, trovins, or troviants), odd spherical sandstone concretions found in the Carpathian region of Romania. The hosts cover why they look alive: they appear to grow, calve off smaller rocks, and seem to move. They describe their history of being mistaken for dinosaur eggs or alien pods, and the 2008 Oslo International Geological Congress finding that they are not true concretions because they lack a nucleus and are made of calcium carbonate sandstone. They explain the proposed formation (a prehistoric river depositing sediment, compression, earthquakes in the Middle Miocene) and growth (a pressurized chemical reaction after rain, with the porous stone growing in pockets). A researcher claimed to have filmed one moving about 2.5 millimeters in two weeks, and the hosts compare this to Death Valley sailing stones moved by thin ice sheets. Marine fossils found inside suggest an ancient marine environment. The episode notes the sites at Ostrovu Mare-area villages Ostrov/Otosani and Costesti, the Trovants Natural Reserve in Buzau County (said as Valca County in transcript), and UNESCO protection.

segments.title: Introduction to trovants
segments.summary: Hosts introduce trovants, the pronunciation confusion, and the odd Romanian rocks that appear to grow and calve off smaller rocks.

segments.title: Appearance and early theories
segments.summary: Trovants range from a few grams to boulders around fifteen feet high. Since the eighteenth century people guessed they were dinosaur eggs or alien pods before geologists examined them as concretions.

segments.title: Oslo 2008 finding: not concretions
segments.summary: At the 2008 International Geological Congress in Oslo, researchers said trovants are not concretions because they lack a nucleus and are made of calcium carbonate sandstone.

segments.title: Proposed formation
segments.summary: Hypothesized formation: a prehistoric river carried minerals into sediment, gravity and Middle Miocene earthquakes compressed the sandstone, producing the rounded shapes.

segments.title: How trovants grow
segments.summary: After rain, trovants absorb minerals that react with the calcium carbonate inside, creating pressure that grows pockets in the porous stone and makes pieces fall off, which looks like birth.

segments.title: Growth rate and filmed movement
segments.summary: Growth is roughly an inch and a half to two inches per thousand years. A researcher claimed to have filmed a trovant moving about 2.5 millimeters over two weeks.

segments.title: Sailing stones of Death Valley
segments.summary: Hosts explain that rocks can move through natural forces, comparing trovants to the Death Valley sailing stones pushed by thin ice sheets.

segments.title: Marine fossils and ancient ocean
segments.summary: Marine fossils such as bivalves and gastropods inside trovants, plus calcium carbonate, suggest the area was once a marine environment.

segments.title: Where trovants are found and protection
segments.summary: Trovants are concentrated in the Trovants Natural Reserve area and in Otosani and Costesti villages in Romania. UNESCO protects them, and visitors are told not to take them.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the short episode and the iHeartRadio credit runs.
